results.title: Australia Post's surprise delivery fees 'killing' some small businesses
results.author: Adelaide Miller
results.content:
Small businesses are being hit with extra fees from Australia Post, which they argue are unfair and eating into already shrinking profit margins.
The ABC has spoken to numerous business owners who regularly send parcels to their customers and have been stung by "underpaid postage fees".
This happens when Australia Post claims the business owner did not pay enough postage and sends an invoice for "underpaid" fees after the parcel has been shipped or delivered.
Future parcels cannot be sent until the fees are paid, forcing business owners to pay up or risk putting their business on hold.
Fashion boutique owner Sam Kemp, based in regional Victoria, said these additional fees were unjustified and financially stressful.
"We are absorbing these costs within our business … it's silently killing small businesses," Ms Kemp said.
One legal expert said this practice by Australia Post could breach its contract, depending on the circumstances.
"If the small business has underpaid according to the terms with Australia Post, [then] Australia Post can ask for the fee to be made up … it has a right to claim the fee," said Melbourne University professor Jeannie Paterson, who specialises in consumer protection law.
"But if Australia Post is claiming a fee it's not entitled to … [it would] possibly mean that Australia Post is either in breach of contract, is engaging in a fraudulent practice, or it's at least engaging in misleading conduct in relation to its customers."
In a statement to the ABC, an Australia Post spokesperson said: "Australia Post processes hundreds of millions of parcels each year, with the vast majority accurately assessed for size and weight using sophisticated automation technology.
"Our automatic size and weight scanning technology is highly accurate, checked daily and independently verified in line with the National Measurement Act. This ensures a consistent, fair approach for all customers and helps maintain efficiency and safety of our network."
Automatic process needs to be accurate
Every dollar counts for small businesses, which operate with some of the slimmest profit margins in the country.
It's why every time Sunshine Coast business owner Emma Kenney receives an underpaid postage fee, it's stressful.
"The financial impact of the underpaid postage fees is actually enormous, and it can take the whole profit from a package that I've sent out," Ms Kenney, who sells women's and kids' clothing and accessories, said.
Feeling unfairly targeted, Ms Kenney spent several hours disputing dozens of her underpaid fees online.
To her surprise, Australia Post dropped several of those charges.
One email from Australia Post said: "I have reviewed the scans, and I can see two different sets of dimensions and weight recorded … I believe another parcel has moved closer to your [sic] causing the incorrect reading."
"I have removed the under paid postage fees of [sic] from your account, and you no longer need to pay this."
Although Australia Post uses an automatic size and weight scanning technology, which it claims is "highly accurate", it would not tell ABC News the error rate due to commercial confidentiality.
Professor Paterson said transparency around this data was important and that if Australia Post made a mistake, there needed to be "a straightforward process" to dispute it.
'Double dipping' allegations
Frustrated by unpaid postage fees, small business owner Sam Kemp lodged an online survey to see whether other businesses were also affected.
More than 170 businesses responded, with fees ranging from a few a month to more than 10 a week, costing businesses between $100 and $30,000.
"I have done everything possible to work with Australia Post … I've changed my bags, I've changed the way we send parcels, and still I am getting [charged] underpaid fees," she said.
"How is that fair to then come back after I have been quoted and paid a shipping fee, and then you're coming back to double dip because you don't think I've paid enough?"
If left unchecked, Professor Paterson warned errors within automatic systems could become "systemic".
"If Australia Post is using an automated system, it's doing that for efficiency grounds, but it has the capacity to make that system very accurate," she said.
"Any automated system needs to have good governance, safeguards, human oversight, and one of those good governance steps is to be monitoring false positives, and indeed false negatives, to make sure the system is performing as accepted."
Complaint with the Ombudsman
Ms Kemp has lodged a complaint with the Commonwealth Ombudsman and is waiting on an outcome.
Speaking broadly, a spokesperson for the Ombudsman said in 2025–26, it received a small number of complaints related to small businesses and underpaid postage fees, making up less than 0.5 per cent of total Postal Industry Ombudsman complaints in the financial year.
"Given the small number of complaints, the office is not currently undertaking or considering a systemic investigation into this issue, but is aware of community concerns," the spokesperson said.
But Professor Paterson said that did not necessarily mean it was a minor problem, and that more data was needed.
"It may be [that] underpaid postage fees are not a significant system issue … or it may be small businesses don't consider complaining is worthwhile or don't realise they have been charged on a flawed basis," she said.
The Ombudsman said it first raised concerns with Australia Post about billing issues for business customers in 2024.
"As a result, Australia Post implemented a range of operational improvements including adjusting tolerance levels on scanning equipment, introducing controls to avoid more than one parcel being weighed at a time, and strengthening calibration and record-keeping processes," the spokesperson said.
results.summary:
Australian small businesses are reporting financial strain due to disputed "underpaid postage" fees issued by Australia Post following automated parcel weight and dimension scans during the shipping process.

### Key Points
- Business owners report receiving retroactive invoices for underpaid postage, which can halt their ability to ship future parcels until fees are settled.
- Australia Post utilizes automated scanning technology that it claims is highly accurate and compliant with the National Measurement Act.
- Some business owners have successfully disputed charges after discovering errors, such as multiple parcels being scanned simultaneously by the automated system.
- A survey of over 170 affected businesses revealed individual financial impacts ranging from minor monthly costs to as much as $30,000.
- The Commonwealth Ombudsman is aware of the issue but is not currently conducting a systemic investigation, noting these complaints represent less than 0.5% of total volume.
- Australia Post has implemented operational improvements, including adjusted tolerance levels and enhanced calibration, to address billing concerns raised in 2024.

### Why it Matters
These disputes highlight the potential risks of relying on automated systems for billing without sufficient human oversight or transparent error-reporting mechanisms. For small businesses operating on thin margins, these unexpected costs can significantly impact profitability and create ongoing operational uncertainty.

results.title: US intelligence advisory names six Chinese AI firms and lists the US models each one targeted
results.author: Alina Maria Stan
results.content:
Three US agencies have jointly named six Chinese AI companies as having systematically extracted capabilities from American frontier models since late 2024, in an advisory detailed enough to list which model each firm went after and how the requests were disguised.
The National Security Agency, the FBI, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency published the advisory on Tuesday under the title “China-Based Artificial Intelligence Companies Conducting Industrial-Scale Distillation Campaigns Against U.S. AI Companies”.
It names DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI. Distillation is the practice of training a cheaper model on the outputs of a more capable one, and the advisory argues it forms “the core, not merely a supplement” of how these companies build.
The sharpest line concerns the number that made DeepSeek a global story. Its widely cited $5.6mn training cost, the advisory says, excludes the cost of data acquired through malicious distillation.
That is a US government document going directly at the claim that convinced markets a frontier model could be built for the price of a house in London.
The company-level detail is unusually specific. DeepSeek is described as running organised campaigns since late 2024 against Claude, Gemini, GPT and Grok models.
Moonshot AI is said to have pulled millions of exchanges from Claude and GPT for its Kimi models from mid-2025. Alibaba is accused of distilling Claude and GPT-5 in late 2025 to improve its Qwen family.
MiniMax of extracting chain-of-thought and reinforcement learning data and attempting prompt injection against Claude Code; StepFun of taking reasoning and coding capability across late 2025 and early 2026; and Z.AI of extracting billions of tokens from GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus by the middle of this year.
How the traffic was routed is the part the industry will read twice. The advisory describes fraudulent account creation, single accounts used across many addresses, requests pushed through cloud providers and third-party aggregators that strip identifying metadata, and what it calls a grey market of API proxies known as transfer stations that defeat geographic restrictions and traceability.
It also describes jailbreak prompts that ask a model to imagine and narrate the reasoning behind an answer it has already given, which is a way of extracting hidden chain-of-thought that the provider never intended to sell. When one route was blocked, the advisory says, operators failed over to another automatically.
On the question everyone will ask, the wording is careful. The campaigns ran “likely with Chinese government awareness”.
That is awareness, not direction, and it is hedged. An advisory this specific about technique being this cautious about attribution is worth noticing rather than rounding up.
One recommendation deserves more scrutiny than it will get. Alongside detection systems and cross-industry intelligence sharing, the agencies suggest providers deploy responses that subtly alter output to suspected distillers without telling them, while informing legitimate researchers.
That is a government body advising private companies to quietly degrade service for users they suspect but have not proven anything against, and every false positive is an ordinary customer being fed worse answers with no way to know.
A Chinese embassy spokesman, Liu Chang, dismissed the allegations as a deliberate attack on China’s development in AI, according to Bloomberg, which first reported the advisory. None of the six companies responded to requests for comment.
TNW reported in April, when the White House first raised industrial-scale distillation as a policy concern, naming three of these companies, and in the same period Anthropic publicly accused Alibaba of running the largest distillation campaign against Claude.
What has changed is the venue. A policy complaint has become a technical advisory from three agencies with per-model attribution attached, which is the form these things take shortly before sanctions are discussed.

Get the most important tech news in your inbox each week.
results.summary:
The NSA, FBI, and CISA have issued a joint advisory accusing six Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing intellectual property from American frontier models through industrial-scale data distillation.

### Key Points
- The advisory identifies DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI as companies conducting unauthorized data extraction campaigns.
- Targeted U.S. models include GPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok, with firms allegedly using fraudulent accounts and API proxies to bypass security restrictions.
- Distillation techniques involve training cheaper models on the outputs of more capable systems, including hidden chain-of-thought reasoning and reinforcement learning data.
- The report claims DeepSeek’s low training costs were achieved by excluding the value of data acquired through these malicious distillation efforts.
- U.S. agencies recommend that AI providers deploy subtle output degradation for suspected malicious users to protect proprietary model capabilities.

### Why it Matters
This technical advisory marks a significant escalation in U.S. efforts to curb the unauthorized transfer of AI technology to Chinese firms. By providing specific evidence of model exploitation, the government is signaling that future trade sanctions or stricter export controls may be imminent.

results.title: "You can never see outside of yourself": The House Before is a body horror game in which you are a house tunnelling through its own soul
results.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
results.content:
It's a lovely morning in the village, and you are a horrible house. Wait, let's start that again. As Gregor Samsa awoke one morning from uneasy dreams he found himself transformed into a horrible house. Wait, let's start that again: "You wake up as a House. Your limbs stretch through endless rooms filled with grotesque creatures. You can never see outside of yourself, never feel the world that lies beyond the fleshy walls of your body. You manage your insides as best you can, but you wonder: are you a good house or just a pale afterthought of the House Before?"
So goes the blurb for The House Before, an atypical body horror game from Gabriel Helfenstein and the art collective Fantasia Malware, which combines elements from visual novels and text adventure with a lot of lurid minigames. It's a journey through your own architectural guts that appears to span a variety of genres: first-person maze games, virtual pet games, top-down tile-based exploration. There are also some bespoke, eminently proddable interface designs that make me think of 90s game installers and virtual desktop music players.
The opening suggestion of being trapped inside your own form is wonderfully claustrophobic, but this seems like lighthearted pastiche in other respects. The creatures you'll meet are both garrulous and colourful. I swore never to idly compare things to vapo(u)rwave again, but I cannot deny the innermost yearnings of my soul: the aesthetics are quite vapo(u)rwavey in places. Look at those shimmering, oily pinks and purples on the "clock" screen. At other times, it's less of a shimmer, more of an ooze, and I think of Nickelodeon. In general, I'm always eager to play games that are ghastly and inventive composites.
The House Before is out November on Steam and Itch.io (the latter's store page isn't yet live as of writing). "If you enjoy short stories such as The Red Tower by Thomas Ligotti or games such as Growing My Grandpa! by Yames, The House Before is for you," notes a press release.
Here is what Alice O (RPS in peace) wrote about Growing My Grandpa!, back in 2024: "You can feed him everything a grandpa needs to grow up strong and healthy: stale cashews, brown bananas, fibreglass insulation, the usual grandpa foods. And absolutely you can even talk with your dear grandpa, once he grows a mouth." Here is a complementary gobbet from Ligotti's The Red Tower: "We are all talking and thinking about the Red Tower in our own degenerate way. I have only recorded what everyone is saying (though they may not know they are saying it), and sometimes what they have seen (though they may not know they have seen it)."
The press release adds that The House Before "won't be for everyone", even though it'll be pretty short at a few hours. I don't know what they're on about. Who wouldn't want to be the absolute worst house? If you prefer your houses to be more cheerful and flirtatious, there's always Building Relationships.
Helfenstein's previous games include North, from way back in 2016. Janksta backstabber Brendy (RPS in peace, grudgingly) wrote about North in one of his free game round-ups, which harbours a few other specimens of note.
results.summary:
Developer Gabriel Helfenstein and art collective Fantasia Malware are set to release The House Before, a surreal body horror game where players navigate a sentient, architectural nightmare.

### Key Points
- The House Before launches this November on Steam and Itch.io.
- Gameplay blends visual novel elements, text adventures, and diverse minigames like first-person mazes.
- The game features a distinct aesthetic described as a mix of vaporwave, 90s software interfaces, and Nickelodeon-style visuals.
- It is marketed as a short, experimental experience for fans of surreal horror works like Thomas Ligotti’s The Red Tower.
- The project follows developer Gabriel Helfenstein’s previous title, the 2016 game North.

### Why it Matters
This title represents a growing trend of experimental, short-form indie games that prioritize unique aesthetic experiences over traditional mechanics. By blending disparate genres into a cohesive body horror narrative, the developers are targeting a niche audience interested in unconventional, art-driven interactive storytelling.

results.title: The Legacy of 9/11: A Surveillance Society
results.author: Robert Kuttner
results.content:
When the attacks of September 11, 2001, stunned America 25 years ago, the Prospect had just moved to Washington and brought on a new executive editor in Harold Meyerson. In about a week, we managed to assign and edit an issue that was one of our best ever. The cover line was “Defending an Open Society.”
The articles in that issue challenged the widespread assumption that we were now in a new normal, in which the vulnerability of an open society had been horribly revealed. Painful as it might be, America supposedly had to sacrifice some liberty to regain some security.
Then as now, that premise was disastrously wrong. But over 25 years, America ended up needlessly sacrificing both.
At the time, it seemed that the ability of a cell of terrorists to pass unnoticed, and to seize and weaponize not one but four jetliners almost simultaneously, demonstrated the pathetic vulnerability of the United States. But as testimony to the 9/11 Commission later revealed, American counterintelligence knew everything it needed to know in 2000 and 2001 to prevent the 9/11 attacks. The problem was that the White House under George W. Bush and Dick Cheney was obsessively focused on Saddam Hussein and didn’t want to know about al-Qaeda in the U.S.
Richard Clarke, director of counterterrorism for the National Security Council, had urgently requested a meeting of NSC principals on January 25, 2021, in a memo during Bush’s first week in office, to develop a comprehensive strategy against jihadists in America. He was rebuffed. Over the next several months, Clarke’s team assembled evidence of a planned attack, pilots being trained, and sleeper cells, but the White House kept fending him off.
Had the Supreme Court not intervened to steal the election for Bush, and had Al Gore been president, Clarke’s urgent warning would almost surely have been taken seriously and 9/11 never would have occurred. We had all the counterintelligence surveillance we needed. We just didn’t have a president who was paying attention.
In the panic that followed the attacks, a wish list of every previously rejected bad idea for warrantless surveillance and spying on Americans was hastily assembled. This became the USA PATRIOT Act. It was rushed through Congress in a fervor of misplaced patriotism and signed on October 26. It passed the House 357-66, and the Senate 98-1. Russ Feingold of Wisconsin, the lone Senate dissenter, warned in a powerful floor speech, “Preserving our freedom is one of the main reasons that we are now engaged in this new war on terrorism. We will lose that war without firing a shot if we sacrifice the liberties of the American people.”
Among other odious items in the administration’s anti-terrorism bill, as Georgetown Law professor David Cole wrote in the Prospect’s 9/11 issue, were provisions to make aliens “deportable not for terrorist activity but for peaceful and nonviolent associational activity … It would authorize the Immigration and Naturalization Service to detain immigrants indefinitely on the attorney general’s say-so, even when they have a legal right to live here permanently and cannot be deported. And it would resurrect the doctrine of ideological exclusion by allowing aliens to be denied entry for their speech.”
All of this, of course, prefigured President Trump’s grotesque anti-immigrant measures.
Today on TAP
This story first appeared in our free Today on TAP newsletter, a weekday email featuring commentary on the daily news from Prospect reporters.
Meanwhile, one of the genuine vulnerabilities that did need attention—international money laundering by terrorists—was remedied by the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020. But the same politicians who support surveillance of citizens and consumers are big supporters of crypto, which is a gift to terrorists and criminals who launder money.
One of the little-noticed consequences of the post-9/11 hysteria has been a diabolical symbiosis between government surveillance and corporate surveillance. What Shoshana Zuboff was the first to call surveillance capitalism has now become ubiquitous, as platform monopolies like Amazon and Google vacuum up customer data to sell targeted ads, screw rivals, and use personalizing pricing.
As the big tech monopolies pursue these surveillance strategies, experience gained in the national security establishment is highly prized. At least 200 people from counterintelligence posts have gone to work for Google, Facebook, and Amazon.
They include Caroline Atkinson, President Obama’s deputy national security adviser for international economics (2011–2015). She subsequently became head of global policy at Google. Robert Kimmitt, general counsel and executive secretary of the National Security Council, went to Facebook. Brian Walsh, special assistant to the president and senior director for intelligence at the National Security Council, went to a senior post at Amazon Web Services. And dozens more.
And the revolving door works both ways, with Trump’s top science, technology, and national security staff coming from Big Tech. What both sectors have in common is a commitment to surveillance.
None of this makes Americans more secure. It makes us more vulnerable.
results.summary:
Reflecting on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, this analysis examines how the U.S. government’s post-9/11 security policies eroded civil liberties while failing to enhance national safety.

### Key Points
- The 9/11 Commission found that U.S. counterintelligence possessed sufficient information to prevent the attacks, but the George W. Bush administration prioritized other geopolitical concerns.
- Richard Clarke, the National Security Council’s counterterrorism director, unsuccessfully urged the White House to address al-Qaeda threats throughout early 2001.
- The USA PATRIOT Act, signed October 26, 2001, authorized expanded government surveillance and indefinite detention of immigrants, with Senator Russ Feingold casting the sole dissenting vote.
- A "revolving door" exists between national security agencies and Big Tech firms like Google, Amazon, and Facebook, which share a common interest in mass data surveillance.
- Modern surveillance capitalism, characterized by corporate data harvesting, has created a symbiotic relationship between government intelligence and private sector monopolies.

### Why it Matters
The expansion of surveillance powers after 9/11 fundamentally altered the relationship between the American government, private corporations, and individual privacy. This shift has created a permanent infrastructure for monitoring citizens that persists today, often prioritizing data collection over actual national security.

results.title: Bernie Sanders backs a 32-hour work week as a German employer pushes to expand to 40 hours — what the data says
results.author: Kit Pulliam
results.content:
Bernie Sanders backs a 32-hour work week as a German employer pushes to expand to 40 hours — what the data says
Vermont Independent Senator Bernie Sanders says it's time to switch to a four-day workweek, while German company Stihl wishes Germany could go back to 40 hours per week.
Both of them want worker pay to stay the same.
Must Read
-       Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one
-       Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP
-       The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes
"It's time to reduce the stress level in our country and allow Americans to enjoy a better quality of life," said Sanders in an op-ed. "It's time for a 32-hour work week with no loss in pay."
Meanwhile, Stihl has argued for the opposite; it wants to rescind Germany's long-held 35-hour work week for the company's metalworkers.
"We no longer have the productivity advantage over key competitors that used to justify our high labour costs," said Nikolas Stihl, who works as the chairman for the chainsaw company Stihl, to Euronews. "That is why I advocate increasing weekly working hours to 40, without any pay compensation."
Here's where both Sanders and Stihl are coming from — and which groups win if either of them get their way.
The 40-hour work week was a huge win for unions
Both the U.S.'s 40-hour work week and Germany's 35-hour work week for metalworkers came from hard-fought union battles for workers' rights.
The National Labor Union — the first one of its kind in the U.S. — was founded in 1866 and quickly started calling for an 8-hour work day. By 1912, the call had coalesced into a movement, complete with a slogan: "Eight hours for work, eight hours for rest and eight hours for what you will."
Thanks to the Great Depression, unions finally got their wish. In 1933, Franklin Delano Roosevelt signed the President's Reemployment Agreement, which encouraged (but did not enforce) a 35-hour work week in the hopes it would cause companies to hire more workers.
In 1938, FDR signed the historic Fair Labor Standards Act, which officially enforced a 40-hour work week. If full-time workers worked more than 40 hours each week, they would have to receive overtime pay.
Germany's 35-hour work week is comparatively newer; metalworkers won it in 1995, after a six-and-a-half week strike in the 1980s that also centered around growing unemployment in the industry.
But some people — including billionaires and company leaders — are unhappy about both of these wins.
results.summary:
Senator Bernie Sanders is advocating for a 32-hour workweek in the United States, while German manufacturer Stihl is pushing to increase its employees' weekly hours to 40.

### Key Points
- Senator Bernie Sanders proposes a 32-hour workweek without a reduction in pay to improve the quality of life for American workers.
- Nikolas Stihl, chairman of the chainsaw manufacturer Stihl, argues that increasing hours to 40 is necessary to maintain competitiveness against global rivals.
- The U.S. established the 40-hour workweek through the 1938 Fair Labor Standards Act, which mandated overtime pay for additional hours.
- German metalworkers secured a 35-hour workweek in 1995 following significant labor strikes and negotiations regarding industry unemployment.
- Both proposals highlight the ongoing tension between labor advocates seeking shorter hours and employers prioritizing productivity and cost management.

### Why it Matters
These conflicting proposals reflect a broader global debate regarding the future of labor standards and the balance between worker well-being and corporate productivity. The outcome of these discussions could significantly influence future employment contracts, labor laws, and the operational strategies of multinational companies.

results.title: Mullvad is shutting down its own DNS service because it thinks this free one is better
results.author: Hamed Paydarfar
results.content:
Summary
- Mullvad is shutting down its public encrypted DNS servers and financially supporting the nonprofit Quad9 instead.
- Mullvad VPN users are unaffected, while default Mullvad Browser configurations will migrate to Quad9 automatically.
- Manually configured users must switch before November 2, 2026; Quad9 offers encrypted DNS, malicious-domain blocking, and strong privacy protections.
Mullvad is shutting down its free public encrypted DNS servers and putting its money behind Quad9 instead. In an official announcement, the privacy-focused VPN provider called Quad9 the “undisputed leader” in public DNS and told people using its servers manually to switch before November 2, 2026.
The closure doesn't affect Mullvad VPN configurations. Those already use Mullvad's internal DNS inside the encrypted VPN tunnel. If you use the browser version (or the included ad-blocking option) with its default DNS-over-HTTPS setting, Mullvad will switch to Quad9 automatically. Custom configurations will be left alone.
Mullvad would rather fund the specialist than imitate it
Quad9 does more than keep your ISP out of your lookups
DNS is the system that translates a website's name (such as makeuseof.com) into the numerical address computers use to find it. Traditional DNS requests can travel unencrypted and potentially expose the domains you visit to your internet service provider or another observer on the network. DNS over HTTPS encrypts those requests by sending them through an HTTPS connection.
Mullvad has offered its public DoH servers since 2022, including versions that block ads and unwanted domains (e.g. trackers, adult content, etc.). They were useful outside its VPN, where users could encrypt DNS lookups without paying for or connecting to anything.
That said, operating a fast and dependable public resolver around the world requires spending money on specialized infrastructure. Mullvad says that maintaining a parallel service would only reproduce part of what Quad9 already provides, so it will financially support the nonprofit instead. As stated in the company's official announcement:
                        
“Rather than duplicating their efforts to achieve only part of what they do, we're putting those resources toward financially supporting Quad9 instead.”
Kudos to you, Mullvad!
Quad9 combines encrypted DNS with network-level threat blocking. It checks the domains your computer requests access to against threat intelligence and refuses to resolve ones associated with malware, spyware, phishing, and exploit kits. Moreover, it says it doesn't collect or retain your IP addresses, which makes it a more security-focused alternative to merely escaping the DNS server selected by your ISP.
If you have manually entered a Mullvad DoH address, the company says you must replace it. Existing Mullvad DNS profiles on iOS and macOS will also stop working and need to be swapped for Quad9 profiles. If you want the change to cover an entire home network, you can configure DNS on your router instead of changing every computer separately — that's if your router allows it.
results.summary:
Privacy-focused VPN provider Mullvad is shutting down its public encrypted DNS servers by November 2, 2026, shifting its financial support to the nonprofit organization Quad9 instead.

### Key Points
- Mullvad will discontinue its public DNS-over-HTTPS servers to avoid duplicating infrastructure efforts.
- Users with manual DNS configurations must switch to alternative providers before the November 2, 2026, deadline.
- Mullvad VPN users remain unaffected as their traffic is routed through internal, encrypted DNS tunnels.
- Default Mullvad Browser settings will automatically migrate to Quad9, which provides encrypted lookups and threat blocking.
- Quad9 is a nonprofit that blocks domains associated with malware, phishing, and spyware without logging user IP addresses.

### Why it Matters
This transition consolidates resources toward a specialized nonprofit, ensuring users continue to receive robust, privacy-focused DNS protection without redundant service maintenance. By offloading this infrastructure, Mullvad reinforces the industry trend of prioritizing dedicated security experts over proprietary, general-purpose alternatives.

results.title: What Russia’s military elite is preparing for behind closed doors
results.author: RT
results.content:
What Russia’s military elite is preparing for behind closed doors
Every year, Russia publishes a private analytical report intended for a select group of military and defense industry leaders. The Russian Military Yearbook is designed strictly for senior officers, security agency staff, and executives of companies in the defense sector.
Unlike public reports on the state of the armed forces, the Russian Military Yearbook is meant for internal use. It addresses military planning, advancements in weaponry, and developments in the defense industry, along with the key priorities of the Russian military leadership amid ongoing conflicts. Consequently, the yearbook sheds light on the priorities of Russia’s defense apparatus.
Russia’s global plans remain unchanged and are based on two main principles
First principle: Russia should be responsible for the stability and development of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). While Moscow does not harbor imperial ambitions to annex former Soviet republics, Russian politicians and military officials view these nations as vital partners in trade, infrastructure projects, and security.
Therefore, countries of the “post-Soviet space” should not join other political and military blocs, especially the EU and NATO. Such blocs often pressure members to sever ties with Russia and are sometimes directed against Russia.
However, Russia welcomes participation in economic collaboration, such as China’s Belt and Road Initiative. What benefits neighboring countries also benefits Russia due to the close economic ties between them.
“The West is entertaining the idea of creating a geopolitical confrontation arena in the South Caucasus, attempting to push Russia aside from the normalization of relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Rejecting such attempts, the Russian Federation intends to do all it can to protect the region.” 
– Analytical report of the Institute of Contemporary International Studies of the Diplomatic Academy of the Russian Foreign Ministry
Second principle: Moscow views stability through the lens of a “multipolar world.” This refers to a situation in international relations where there is no single hegemon or “world police.” Decisions regarding security and regional organization are made either at the regional level or during global negotiations, rather than by one or two central powers.
It may seem that America’s recent setbacks – including conflicts with European allies and protracted crises in Iran and the Middle East – create an ideal situation for Russian strategists. As Washington’s influence wanes, America’s capacity to control global affairs may diminish as well. However, that perception is wrong.
Russian military and political leaders desire not only a world without hegemony but also one characterized by stability and adherence to international laws. Even setting idealism aside, this approach undeniably serves Russia’s interests. UN principles help maintain the status quo and ensure regional leadership.
Conflicts involving Russia are often caused by breaches of agreements (primarily regarding NATO expansion), leading to the use of force and the disruption of regional balance. This was true of the conflict with Georgia in 2008, the civil war in Syria, and the Ukraine crisis.
Moreover, America’s inability to manage conflicts (which are often instigated by its own government) only serves to destabilize the world. This compels Moscow to allocate more resources for potential interventions. The Kremlin is well aware of what happens when a crisis outside its borders spirals out of control.
“According to S.V. Lavrov, the Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs, ‘The USA could become one of the responsible centers of power together with Russia, China, and other powers of the Global South, East, North, and West in the foreseeable future’, but this is subject to them abandoning the counteraction to the objective process of multipolarity strengthening” 
– Analytical report of the Institute of Contemporary International Studies of the Diplomatic Academy of the Russian Foreign Ministry
Russian analysts do not believe that it is possible to return to the former Western-centric world order. They believe the Trump administration is too preoccupied with internal issues and is consistently souring relations with European allies, whom it views as ‘parasites’. Meanwhile, the EU is becoming increasingly reliant on rigid neoliberal institutions, making it less open to negotiations due to entrenched anti-Russia sentiments among its leaders.
Consequently, the only remaining option is to build a multipolar world.
Moscow sees China and India, as well as the nations of the Global South, as its partners in this new world order. These governments also seek independence from the US and Europe and are pursuing their regional agendas. However, experts point out that Russia’s goals may diverge from those of its partners and could even come into conflict with their goals; no one is willing to sacrifice foreign policy autonomy for the sake of “unconditional friendship.”
Despite the prevailing pessimism surrounding global politics, Russian experts believe that new conflicts can be avoided, even during such troubled times.
However, analysts are concerned about one particular region.
Very Cold War
In addition to the existing conflict zones, experts are also analyzing another potential flashpoint – the struggle for control over the Arctic. And this isn’t just about the vast reserves of valuable resources in the Arctic – estimates suggest that around 13% of the world’s oil and 30% of its natural gas lie beneath the ice.
Disputes over this “no man’s land” and its surrounding waters have been going on for nearly two centuries, and date back to the first attempts to carve out spheres of influence in the Arctic. Canada even attempted to occupy one of Russia’s Arctic islands during the Civil War, though this “occupation” was limited to a few settlers who were soon sent home by the Russian Navy.
Experts note that NATO countries have already begun a major arms buildup specifically aimed at potential Arctic operations. Military exercises are frequently held in the region, such as the recent Exercise Cold Response 26. In March, tens of thousands of service members participated in drills led by the Norwegian armed forces.
“During regular exercises in the Arctic, NATO countries carry out activities to conduct reconnaissance of all types, prepare and deliver missile, air, bomb, and torpedo strikes. Skills related to combat control and logistics, the interaction of dissimilar forces and means are honed.” 
– Vadim Istomin, doctor of Technical Sciences 
And this is just the beginning. NATO countries have initiated Arctic-aimed retraining and rearmament programs set to be completed by the early 2030s. NATO members call it preparation for possible threats. Yet analysts speculate that it could also be preparation for a coordinated attack.
Here are several examples:
Finland – HX / F-35 Program: As a new NATO member, Finland has acquired 64 F-35A fighters, as well as weapons and equipment for Arctic operations. It is also retraining pilots and technical staff. By 2028-2030, the F-35s are expected to fully replace F/A-18 Hornet aircraft.
Canada – North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) modernization: A new threat detection system for the Arctic is being developed. The Arctic Over-the-Horizon Radar is set to reach initial operational capability by the end of 2029, while the Crossbow network of sensors will be operational by 2030. The Polar Over-the-Horizon Radar is anticipated to become operational between 2032 and 2033. Infrastructure for aviation and the command system are also being upgraded.
Canada – Rearmament of the Air Force: Canada is purchasing 88 F-35As to replace its CF-18 fleet. Initial combat readiness is slated for 2029, with full capability set to be reached by 2033. This program aims to enhance the defense of Canada’s Arctic region.
Denmark and Greenland – Defense Program 2024-2033: Military infrastructure in the Arctic and North Atlantic is being strengthened through the acquisition of new Arctic ships and drones, alongside the deployment of additional surveillance assets in Greenland. The Joint Arctic Command is also being bolstered to support extended operations in the area.
This isn’t just speculation. In 2021, the Pentagon adopted a new strategic plan titled ‘Regaining Arctic Dominance’. It explicitly states that the US intends to push Russia and China out of the Arctic, including through threats and the use of force.
“It appears that, distracted by the conflict in Ukraine, the Americans have seemingly pushed the Russian Arctic to the periphery of their attention for the time being. But this is a dangerous delusion. Washington never abandoned the thought of redrawing borders in that area.” 
– Aleksey Fenenko, doctor of Political Science, professor of the Faculty of World Politics, Lomonosov Moscow State University 
In addition to the natural resources and military presence in the Arctic, NATO is interested in the Northern Sea Route. This corridor connects Asia and Europe via the Arctic Ocean, providing a faster alternative to the traditional southern route through India and the Suez Canal. Considering rising piracy and the Iran crisis, navigating the icy waters has become a safer alternative.
However, due to geographical factors, the Northern Sea Route heavily relies on Russian maritime infrastructure, effectively giving Moscow control over ship and cargo movements. Consequently, Russia could dictate terms to carriers or even halt traffic entirely. Of course, NATO doesn’t want this.
Canada is expanding its fleet of icebreakers, and Norwegian spy vessel the FS Marjata is increasingly being spotted in the Barents Sea. Meanwhile, Finland is deploying American F-35A fighters just 150 km from the Russian border. The US is ramping up its military presence in Alaska, launching new NAVSTAR military satellites over the region, and ordering amphibious vehicles, which are ideally suited for operations in the north. Swedish BvS10 Beowulf amphibious tracked all-terrain vehicles are a particularly popular choice.
The Russian military is already preparing for potential conflicts in the Arctic. The Russian Army and Navy traditionally have a strong presence in the North and benefit from developed infrastructure. New missile defense systems ensure aerial security. Tor-M2 missile systems, available in various configurations, also play a significant role. The specialized variant for naval vessels, the Tor-M2KM, is particularly easy to produce in mass quantities.
Russia is ready to respond to any challenge in the Arctic; yet this crisis can still be avoided.
Meanwhile, Russia is forced to address another issue on a daily basis – though one may call it more profitable.
Arms market shakeup
The armaments and military equipment (A&ME) sector, unlike many others, boasts consistent growth in both demand and supply, expanding by 28% over four years to reach $679 billion.
In 2022, the weapons market began to shift dramatically. Sanctions caused Russian exports to plummet from 18% to 12%, with lost contracts primarily shifting to American manufacturers.
The composition of imports has also changed, becoming more unstable and concentrated in regions of existing or potential conflicts. Warsaw has emerged as the world’s leading arms purchaser, spending $33 billion on weaponry in 2023 alone. Given Poland’s status as “NATO’s vanguard,” there’s little doubt about the purpose behind this arms buildup.
Clearly, supplies to Ukraine have significantly increased, but experts point out an important detail: Western allies mainly send legacy military equipment to Kiev, which allows them to quickly modernize their own arsenals. And it’s clear who benefits most from this situation.
“After getting rid of the obsolete weapon systems supplied to Kiev as military aid, the ‘collective West’ countries began large-scale purchases of modern and more expensive arms. At the same time, the USA became the main beneficiary and recipient in this situation, having practically monopolized the arms market of NATO member states.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
Since 2021, the Russian defense industry has grown approximately fivefold (with the output of some sectors increasing by six or even seven times). However, the bulk of this production is consumed by the Russian military, and exports are severely restricted due to sanctions. Nevertheless, analysts believe that after the end of the Special Military Operation, the Russian defense sector may dominate the market.
Experts note that the unique advantage of Russian weaponry developed during the Ukraine crisis is its proven adaptability to real-world battle conditions. Most Western and Asian arsenals have been tested only during military exercises, whereas new Russian models have been designed and adapted based on data gathered from the battlefield.
The primary goal of Russian defense companies was not to create a budget-friendly training model; they needed to design weapons that would prove reliable in real battle conditions. Developers also received ample feedback from soldiers who tested the weapons in battle.
Looking ahead, Saudi Arabia and India are expected to be major buyers of weapons; analysts predict these countries will focus on importing weapons in the coming years. China could also become a major buyer of Russian defense products, though Beijing consistently reduces foreign procurement in favor of satisfying demand through domestic production.
These imports extend beyond just rifles, ammunition, missiles, and aircraft. Analysts forecast that by 2030, 40% of the entire defense market will revolve around technological exchange – selling access to new developments, as well as training engineers and military personnel.
This sector is already evident in Russia’s partnership with India. For instance, Rosoboronexport is working on localizing AK-203 rifles and 125mm Mango APFSDS rounds in India, as well as upgrading T-72 tank engines at Indian facilities.
High-altitude and high-tech
When people discuss Russian military exports, they often think of tanks and Kalashnikov rifles. This makes sense, as the Russian Army is primarily viewed as a land power, and advancements in the development of rifles and tanks indeed play a significant role in its capabilities.
However, the Ukraine conflict has highlighted the crucial importance of air superiority, especially in the age of drone warfare. The Russian military employs a wide array of tools tailored for various tasks.
On the one hand, there are powerful systems like the S-400 Triumph surface-to-air missile system. Adopted by the Russian military in 2007, this system can detect aerial objects up to 600 km away and engage aerodynamic targets at a distance of up to 380 km. This system has repeatedly demonstrated its effectiveness, even though it was designed at a time when warfare was quite different.
“The S-400 Triumph is capable of fighting the entire range of modern air targets within its zone of responsibility. This isn’t only the merit of the developers but also of the General Staff which managed to predict long-term threats.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
But there are also small, mobile systems that are indispensable in urban combat and dynamic modern warfare.
A prime example is the Dzhigit support launcher. Without its Igla-S and Verba missile launchers, it looks like a sophisticated garden chair. However, fully equipped, it can fire powerful missiles in rapid succession or salvos, functioning on the ground, in buildings, or mounted on a combat vehicle. Military personnel particularly appreciate its stealth capabilities and battlefield survivability.
As for new Western radar and missile defense developments, analysts are skeptical about them. They note that while these new models often set records, they don’t necessarily enhance practical use.
“The TRLM-4D is also a leader in the number of simultaneously detected targets – 1500. However, the only thing that such a number of blips on the radar screen can give to the crew having just 24 ADMS is a sense of despair.” 
– Centre for Analysis of World Arms Trade 
Uncertainty is the new certainty
Overall, Russia’s strategy can be summed up as “active preparation for the worst, moderate hope for the best.” Politicians, military leaders, and defense industry representatives understand that the Special Military Operation may continue for an extended period, while adversaries seek to exploit any weaknesses that Russia may have; therefore, new crises are almost inevitable. Recent years have demonstrated the resilience of the Russian military and economy, but that alone may not ensure success.
At the same time, analysts believe that a peaceful resolution to all issues is possible. However, it probably won’t be brought about by the goodwill of politicians, but rather by the demonstration of strength and the readiness to respond to any threats.

results.title: The Death Of The Button: Why The Best Interface Is No Interface
results.author: hello@smashingmagazine.com (Carrie Webster)
results.content:
Ever since the commercialisation of the Graphical User Interface pioneered by systems like the Xerox Star and popularised by the original Apple Macintosh, software has relied heavily on point-and-click interactions. If you wanted to book a trip, buy a pair of shoes, or research a health symptom, you were expected to navigate a labyrinth of user interfaces. You click menus, adjust range sliders, fill out multi-step forms, deal with cookie pop-ups, and open dozens of browser tabs just to cross-reference basic information. We have become accustomed to spending more time managing the software rather than actually achieving our goals.
That contract is officially changing. Driven by advances in artificial intelligence and large language models, a new generation of web tools is pioneering a radical philosophy: Intent-Driven Design. Rather than expecting our users to learn complex menus and click through elaborate sales funnels, these platforms operate by capturing high-level human goals and silently executing the grunt work in the background.
This vision builds on long-standing HCI concepts like Golden Krishna’s “The Best Interface Is No Interface” and Don Norman’s principles of human-centered design.
“
Well, at least what we understand based on our current experience.
It is essential for UX designers to understand the changes we’re witnessing and even re-evaluate our role, shifting our focus from designing visible interfaces to guiding transparent, intent-driven AI experiences.
The Death Of The “10-click” Process
To understand where web design is going, we first have to look at the friction we have accepted as “normal” for decades.
Consider the traditional workflow of buying a flight online. The user experience is intentionally hyper-interactive:
- Navigate to a travel aggregator or airline website.
- Select “Round Trip” from a dropdown menu.
- Type the origin city and wait for auto-complete.
- Type the destination city and wait for auto-complete.
- Click a calendar modal, toggle through months, and select departure and return dates.
- Choose the number of passengers and cabin class.
- Click “Search” and wait for the results page to load.
- Filter by price, layover duration, departure time, and airline.
- Sort the results and scan through dozens of individual options.
- Click through a three-page checkout funnel dodging upsells for rental cars and travel insurance.
This is a classic point-and-click UI paradigm. The computer acts as a passive container of data, and the human acts as the orchestrator, manually inputting parameters, interpreting raw outputs, and executing each micro-step along the way.
Intent-driven design flips this dynamic entirely. Instead of forcing you to navigate the mechanical steps of how to find a flight, the interface asks a simple question: What are you trying to accomplish?
When you express a goal, such as “Find me a non-stop flight to Chicago next weekend under $300 that arrives before 5 PM”, the software reads your intent, executes the multi-step search query behind the scenes, compares the options, and presents a single actionable resolution. The ten clicks dissolve into one clear intent outcome.
Three Web Platform Examples Replacing Buttons With Intent
This shift isn’t a theoretical vision of the distant future. Some of the world’s most accessible websites allow you to experience intent-capturing systems already.
1. Perplexity AI: Search Without The Open Tabs
Traditional search engines like Google were built as directories. You typed a keyword, and the interface rewarded you with ten blue links. The actual work of opening five tabs, skimming long articles, dodging ads, and manually assembling an answer was left to you. Although this is now changing, with AI content appearing first when you search on Google.
Perplexity AI allows anyone to perform instant intent-based searches. Instead of forcing you to click into multiple tabs, the interface synthesises the perfect result for your context.
- The interaction: You ask a complex question in plain English: “Compare the top three budget laptops for a computer science student, focusing on battery life and keyboard quality.”
- The invisible work: In under two seconds, the platform searches the web, reads dozens of articles, evaluates hardware specifications, and cross-references user reviews.
- The result: (See screen above) Instead of throwing web pages at you, Perplexity dynamically generates a single custom answer complete with formatted comparison tables, pros and cons lists, and concise inline citations. You get the outcome of thirty clicks in just one.
2. Vercel v0: Web Design Without Dragging And Dropping
For years, creating a website meant using visual builders like Figma or drag-and-drop web editors. As designers, we spent hours manually drawing rectangles, picking hexadecimal colour codes, adjusting padding values, and sometimes writing CSS code.
Vercel v0 lets anyone test its generative interface builder right from the home page without signing in.
- The Interaction: A user types a descriptive goal into the input prompt: “Create a modern dark-mode dashboard for a subscription SaaS app showing monthly revenue, active users, and a customer churn chart.”
- The invisible work: The underlying AI understands layout principles, accessibility guidelines, UI component libraries, and responsiveness. It writes clean HTML, Tailwind CSS, and React code in real time.
- The result: Rather than spending an afternoon manipulating elements, the user receives a fully functional, pixel-perfect user interface in seconds! The traditional visual design tool disappears, replaced by raw human intent.
3. Goblin.tools: Breaking Down Overwhelming Tasks
Many traditional productivity tools require you to manually construct task lists, drag items across Kanban boards, and assign micro-deadlines. Goblin.tools is a free, single-page suite of single-task AI tools designed specifically for neurodivergent users or anyone feeling overwhelmed, requiring zero sign-ups or configuration.
- The interaction: You enter a vague, intimidating goal into the Magic Todo tool, such as “Prepare for a job interview”.
- The invisible work: Instead of forcing you to plan every step, the system analyses the cognitive load of the goal and automatically breaks it down into small, actionable sub-tasks adjusted to your preferred level of detail.
- The result: The interface eliminates the stressful task-planning phase and presents a clean checklist tailored to your exact goal.
The Core Pillars Of Intent-driven Web Design
When you remove traditional menus, sidebars, and forms, how do you keep a website usable? Designers pioneering this space rely on three core pillars:
| Pillar | Traditional UX approach | Intent-driven UX approach | 
|---|---|---|
| User input | Micro-actions (Clicks, dropdowns, toggles) | 1. High-level goals (Natural language, context, habits) | 
| Interface state | Static layouts (Everyone sees the same page) | 2. Generative UI (Layouts created dynamically on the fly) | 
| Task execution | Manual execution by the user | 3. Autonomous execution by background AI agents | 
1. High-level Goals
An invisible interface doesn’t always wait for you to type a command — it leverages context to anticipate user needs. Guided by industry standards like Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines on Contextual & Ambient Design, modern systems read environmental metadata, such as device state, location, and past interaction patterns, to trigger proactive actions.
For example:
- Time and location: A food delivery web app prioritising your saved home address and dinner items automatically at 6:30 PM on a weekday.
- Cross-app history: A calendar application noticing an email about an upcoming appointment and surfacing a one-click “Add to Schedule” card without forcing you to copy and paste event details manually.
2. Generative UI
In traditional web design, every user sees the exact same layout. An e-commerce store shows the same navigation bar whether you are a first-time visitor looking for customer support or a returning customer tracking a package.
As highlighted in the Nielsen Norman Group’s analysis on AI as a new UX paradigm, computing is shifting from command-based interaction to outcome-specification. This enables Generative UI, where interfaces are rendered dynamically on the fly based on what you are trying to do in that exact moment. For example, platforms like Vercel v0 demonstrate how raw intent can instantly render functional code components without manual layout building. If you express a desire to compute complex financial data, the interface generates a dynamic calculator widget on demand, receding once your goal is completed.
3. Execution by AI Agents
Traditional interfaces are obsessed with prevention, constantly peppering users with confirmation pop-ups (“Are you sure you want to delete this file?”).
Intent-driven interfaces adapt Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics on User Control and Error Recovery by shifting the safety net from prevention to easy reversibility. Because autonomous agents take actions on your behalf, products prioritise frictionless rollback mechanisms. A prominent “Undo” button, simple revision prompts (“Make this summary shorter”), and transparent audit logs replace intrusive warning modals.
The Hidden Risks
While removing interface friction is liberating, stripping away visual controls introduces significant product design challenges. When software acts on inferred intent rather than direct point-and-click commands, designers must navigate critical ethical and technical pitfalls.
The Illusion Of Control
When a website makes decisions for you, it can quickly feel patronising or invasive. As explored by the Stanford Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) Group, automation must maintain clear boundaries to prevent user frustration. Furthermore, ethical frameworks from the Center for Humane Technology emphasise that product designers must guard against manipulative defaults.
Designers must strike a delicate balance: automate routine execution, but explicitly prompt the user for high-stakes confirmations (such as financial transactions, publishing public content, or altering privacy settings).
The Black Box Problem
In a traditional UI, if you get an unexpected result, you can usually diagnose the issue — perhaps you checked the wrong filter box or selected an incorrect date.
With an intent-driven interface, troubleshooting becomes harder. To address this “black box” challenge, the Google PAIR (People + AI Research) Guidebook advocates for transparent feedback loops. The system must explicitly state its interpretation (“Searching for non-stop flights to Chicago under $300…”) so users can calibrate trust and correct misinterpretations instantly.
From A UX Perspective
As a UX designer, always being curious to understand how our design approach is changing in the world of AI, I find it essential that we re-evaluate the foundational elements of our craft.
“
By mastering these evolving patterns, like ambient feedback, inline prompts, and transparent AI status indicators, we can ensure that screenless, agent-driven tools remain intuitive, ethical, and deeply human-centered.
Conclusion
The ultimate goal: The best design is no design.
For decades, the digital industry has evaluated software success through engagement metrics like time spent in app, click-through rates, and page views per session. Websites were deliberately engineered to maximise visual engagement and interaction volume.
The philosophy behind Golden Krishna’s seminal book The Best Interface Is No Interface, aligned with the broader Center for Humane Technology’s Time Well Spent movement, turns these metrics on their head. The ultimate test of a modern digital product is no longer how visually captivating its buttons are, but rather: How effectively did this software solve the problem and get out of the user’s way?,
We are entering an era where web applications will no longer be measured by the beauty of their interfaces, but by their ability to render those complex interfaces completely obsolete. The future of the web isn’t more interaction — it is seamless, invisible completion.
results.summary:
Intent-driven design is replacing traditional point-and-click web interfaces with AI-powered systems that execute complex tasks based on user goals rather than manual navigation through menus and forms.

### Key Points
- Intent-driven design shifts software interaction from manual micro-steps to high-level goal expression using natural language.
- Platforms like Perplexity AI, Vercel v0, and Goblin.tools demonstrate how AI can synthesize information, generate code, and organize tasks autonomously.
- The approach relies on three pillars: high-level goal processing, generative UI that adapts to user needs, and autonomous execution by background AI agents.
- Designers are moving away from static layouts toward ambient, context-aware interfaces that prioritize frictionless outcomes over engagement metrics like click-through rates.
- Ethical challenges include the "black box" problem and the need to maintain user control while automating routine digital tasks.

### Why it Matters
This shift represents a fundamental change in how users interact with technology, moving from managing software to achieving outcomes. By prioritizing efficiency over engagement, businesses may see a decline in traditional metrics like time-on-site, but will likely gain significant value through improved user satisfaction and task completion rates.
